subject: literature
passage: Mr. ______ who had been station master at the junction for thirty-one years and had retired on a Friday with a handshake and a clock, was back on the platform the following Monday. He did not wear the uniform. He carried a trowel and a bucket, and he began to dig up the strip of cinders between the waiting room and the fence. The new station master, a young man who kept checking his watch, asked him politely what he was doing. "Planting," said Mr. Okafor, and he did not look up. By June the passengers on the morning train were leaning out of the windows to see the roses.
stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

explanation.why: The subject of the sentence is "Mr. Okafor," and its verb is "was." The clause "who had been station master … a handshake and a clock" is extra information about him. It closes with a comma before "was," so it must open with a comma too; the two marks around extra information must match.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Without an opening comma, the "who" clause is not set off, yet a stray comma then appears before the verb "was."
explanation.B: Incorrect. A semicolon must join two independent clauses, and "Mr. Okafor" alone is not one.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The extra information closes with a comma, so it cannot open with a dash; the two marks must match.
explanation.D: Correct. The opening comma matches the comma before "was," setting off the "who" clause as extra information.
